controversies/mission-and-colonialism/qu: Was modern Christian mission an instrument of colonial empire or the seed of indigenous world Christianity?
controversies/mission-and-colonialism/ti: Mission and colonialism: critique and defence
controversies/mission-and-colonialism/su: Missions accompanied Spanish, Portuguese, British, French and other empires, and critics charge them with cultural imperialism and complicity in conquest. Defenders and many historians argue that missionaries also resisted abuses, translated Scripture into local languages and empowered indigenous Christians who soon outgrew missionary control.
controversies/mission-and-colonialism/si: Missionaries arrived with gunboats, treaties and racial hierarchies. They condemned local religions, dress and family structures as heathen, served colonial administrations through schools and hospitals, and kept indigenous Christians subordinate (as with Bishop Crowther). Residential schools, forced conversions in the Americas and the Requerimiento show that the cross and the sword often travelled together.

The colonial story is real but not the whole story. Missionaries translated the Bible into hundreds of languages, gave peoples written literatures and schools, and often fought colonial injustice. Above all, African, Asian and Latin American Christians received the faith on their own terms, made it their own and spread it far beyond missionary control, which is why Christianity grew fastest after empire ended.
Converts’ agency does not excuse missionaries
controversies/mission-and-colonialism/ti: Spanish conquest and the beginning of colonial missions in the Americas.
Evangelical campaign secures abolition of the British slave trade.

Edinburgh conference, dominated by Western delegates.

controversies/mission-and-colonialism/re: Historians now generally describe a mixed and ambivalent relationship between missions and empire. Churches have apologised for specific harms (e.g. Canadian residential schools, papal apology 2022), while world Christianity scholarship stresses indigenous agency.

Rise of world Christianity as a field of study.
controversies/fundamentalist-modernist-c: Can Christianity be reinterpreted for modern knowledge without ceasing to be Christianity?

In the early 20th century, especially in American Presbyterian and Baptist churches, liberals (modernists) sought to reconcile faith with historical criticism and evolution, while fundamentalists insisted on non-negotiable supernatural doctrines. The conflict reshaped Protestantism into mainline and evangelical camps.

Faith must not require intelligent people to reject what they know about history and science. The abiding experiences of Christianity (trust in God, the way of Jesus, love) can be expressed in changing categories. The church should have room for those who cannot hold a literal virgin birth or inerrant Bible but who love Christ.
Tolerance and liberty within the church

Christianity is a historical, redemptive religion: if Christ was not born of a virgin, did not die for our sins and rise bodily, there is no gospel. Liberalism uses Christian words for a different religion. Honesty requires that those who reject the church’s confessions not occupy its pulpits.

Both sides grounded faith in something human: liberals in experience, fundamentalists in a theory of the text. The Word of God is Jesus Christ himself, who speaks through Scripture in sovereign freedom and judges both our modern culture and our religious certainties.
A. A. Hodge and B. B. Warfield publish "Inspiration", defining inerrancy of the original autographs.
Charles A. Briggs suspended from the Presbyterian ministry over higher criticism.
Presbyterian "five fundamentals"; The Fundamentals begin publication.
Auburn Affirmation defends theological liberty in the Presbyterian Church.
Princeton Seminary reorganised; Machen founds Westminster Seminary.
Conservative resurgence begins in the Southern Baptist Convention.

Modernists retained control of the northern mainline denominations; fundamentalists withdrew into separate churches and institutions, from which neo-evangelicalism later emerged. The result was the enduring mainline/evangelical divide in American Protestantism.
Created the two-party structure of American Protestantism.
Shaped American debates on evolution and education.
Fed later denominational splits and the Religious Right.
controversies/was-there-a-great-apostasy: Did the historic Church fall into apostasy, requiring a restoration?
Restoration claims and the historic churches

Many 19th-century American movements (Stone-Campbell Restorationists, Latter-day Saints, Adventists, Bible Students) held that the historic Church had departed from New Testament Christianity. Some sought to restore primitive practice within Nicene faith; others (Latter-day Saints, Jehovah’s Witnesses) rejected the Nicene creed itself and are classed by the historic churches as outside orthodoxy.

Christians are divided because they built creeds and traditions on top of Scripture. Let us lay them aside and restore the simple faith and practice of the New Testament church: immersion of believers, the Lord’s Supper each week, elders in each congregation and the name "Christian" alone.
The Bible needs a rule of faith

After the apostles died, priesthood authority was lost. God the Father and his Son appeared to Joseph Smith and restored the Church with prophets, apostles, priesthood and further scripture. The Book of Mormon is another testament of Jesus Christ.
Departure from biblical monotheism and the Nicene Creed

Soon after the apostles, Greek philosophy corrupted the Church with the Trinity, the immortal soul and hellfire. By careful Bible study we have restored the worship of Jehovah, the only true God, through his Son Jesus Christ, and proclaim his kingdom that began ruling in 1914.

Christ promised that the gates of hell would not prevail against his Church and that the Spirit would lead it into all truth. The creeds of Nicaea and Constantinople faithfully express the apostolic faith. Reform within the Church is always needed, but a total apostasy would make Christ’s promise void.
Cane Ridge revival, out of which Barton Stone’s movement grows.

Latter-day Saints and Jehovah’s Witnesses remain outside the communion of Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches, which regard their doctrines of God as incompatible with the Nicene Creed; both movements regard themselves as the restored true Church.

controversies/should-churches-seek-visib: Should divided churches seek visible unity?

The 20th-century ecumenical movement sought to overcome Christian divisions through councils, dialogues and church unions. Evangelicals, fundamentalists, some Orthodox and traditionalist Catholics questioned its methods and goals, while new forms of cooperation emerged.

Christ prayed that his disciples might be one so that the world may believe. Our divisions are a scandal; we must pray, study and work together until we can share one table. Dialogue has already healed disputes that once seemed unbridgeable.
Unity at the expense of truth

True unity is spiritual and grounded in the gospel. We gladly cooperate with all who confess the biblical gospel in evangelism and service, but institutional union with churches that compromise Scripture would sacrifice truth.
Invisible unity is not what Jesus prayed for
Scripture commands separation from those who deny the faith. The ecumenical movement embraces modernism and Rome; faithful churches must stand apart and contend for the truth.
Church of South India unites Anglicans, Methodists and Reformed.
